title: Design a URL Shortener
subtitle: From single server to globally distributed — stage by stage

stages.title: Stage 1 — Just Ship It
stages.bottleneck: Single point of failure. The server handles everything — web, key generation, database. One crash = total outage.
stages.narrative:
**The simplest possible URL shortener.** A single Node.js server takes a long URL, generates a Base62-encoded short key from an auto-incrementing ID, stores the mapping in PostgreSQL, and 302-redirects on lookup.

**Key generation:** `Base62(auto_increment_id)` → 7 characters = 3.5 trillion combinations.

**This works for ~100 req/sec** — a weekend project or internal tool. But one server crash and the entire service goes down.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Separate Read & Write Paths
stages.bottleneck: Database is the bottleneck. 100:1 read-to-write ratio means the single DB is overwhelmed by redirect lookups.
stages.narrative:
**Split the database load.** Since reads outnumber writes 100:1, a read replica handles all redirect lookups while the primary only handles writes.

**Key generation is extracted** to its own service — it pre-generates batches of unique keys so write latency stays flat.

**Replication lag** (~50ms) is acceptable: a URL created 50ms ago failing to resolve is fine. Users retry naturally.

**This handles ~1K req/sec.** But every redirect still hits the database.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Add Caching Layer
stages.bottleneck: Even read replicas can't handle 10K+ redirects/sec. Hot URLs (top 20%) account for 80% of traffic — perfect for cache.
stages.narrative:
**Redis changes the game.** The 80/20 rule: top 20% of URLs serve 80% of redirects. Redis stores these hot mappings in memory — sub-millisecond lookups.

**Cache strategy: Write-around + Read-through.** On new URL creation, don't populate the cache (most URLs are never accessed again). On redirect, check cache → miss → DB → populate cache.

**LRU eviction** with TTL keeps memory bounded. A 10GB Redis instance stores ~50M URL mappings.

**This handles ~10K req/sec** with 95%+ cache hit rate. But what if the app server crashes?

stages.title: Stage 4 — Load Balancer + Horizontal Scale
stages.bottleneck: Single app server is a SPOF. No way to scale compute independently. Need horizontal scaling behind a load balancer.
stages.narrative:
**Horizontal scaling unlocked.** Multiple stateless app servers behind a load balancer. Any server can handle any request — no session state.

**Key generation uses Zookeeper** to assign ID ranges to each server. Server 1 gets [1–1M], Server 2 gets [1M–2M]. No coordination needed for key uniqueness.

**Redis is now a cluster** — sharded by key hash. Data distributed across 3+ nodes with automatic failover.

**Health checks:** the LB pings `/healthz` every 5s. Unhealthy servers are removed from the pool in seconds.

**This handles ~100K req/sec.** But the database is still a single shard.

stages.title: Stage 5 — Shard, CDN, Async Analytics
stages.bottleneck: At 100M+ URLs, a single DB can't hold all mappings. Analytics writes block redirects. Global users experience high latency.
stages.narrative:
**The production architecture.** Every component is now redundant, sharded, and globally distributed.

**CDN caching**: popular short URLs resolved at the edge (< 10ms globally). 301 redirects for permanent URLs, 302 for analytics-tracked ones.

**Database sharding** by consistent hash of the short key. Each shard handles ~50M URLs. Add shards horizontally as data grows.

**Async analytics**: click events pushed to Kafka, batch-processed to a warehouse. Redirect path is never blocked by analytics writes.

**This handles 1M+ req/sec** at 99.99% availability. Cost: ~$5K/month for the core infrastructure.
